      <content name="title">Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Therapy</span></span></span> for Menopause</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">ERT</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Estrogen Replacement <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Therapy</span></span></span></content>

      <content name="altTitle">Menopausal Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Therapy</span></span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> for menopause?<p>Menopause is the time in a woman's life when her menstrual periods stop.  It is a normal part of aging. During menopause, the body makes much lower amounts of the hormones estrogen and progesterone.</p><p>Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> for menopause involves taking estrogen, with or without progesterone (or a similar hormone called progestin). The goal is to replace some of the hormones the body no longer makes and help relieve menopausal symptoms.</p>What does hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> for menopause <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treat</span></span></span>?<p>In the years leading up to menopause, and during menopause, hormone levels can rise and fall. These changes can cause symptoms for some women that may be mild and go away on their own. For others, symptoms may be more severe and affect daily life.</p><p>Lower hormone levels during menopause can cause symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>Hot flashes</li><li>Night sweats</li><li>Mood changes</li><li>Vaginal dryness</li><li>Pain during sex</li></ul><p>Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> may help relieve these symptoms. It may also help protect against osteoporosis.</p>Who should not use hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> for menopause?<p>Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> is not right for everyone. You should not use hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> for menopause if you:</p><ul><li>Are pregnant or think that you may be pregnant</li><li>Have unexplained vaginal bleeding</li><li>Have had certain types of cancer</li><li>Have had a stroke or heart attack</li><li>Have had blood clots</li><li>Have liver disease</li></ul><p>Talk with your health care provider about your medical history before starting hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span>.</p>What are the types of hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> for menopause?<p>There are different types of hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> for menopause. If you had surgery to remove your uterus (hysterectomy) your provider may recommend estrogen only <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span>. If you still have your uterus, your provider may recommend estrogen plus progesterone (or progestin) <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span>.</p><p>Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> for menopause comes in several forms. Most are pills taken by mouth, but there are also skin patches, gels or sprays, vaginal creams, tablets, or rings.</p><p>Your provider can help you choose the type and form that's best for you.</p>What are the risks of hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> for menopause?<p>Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> has some risks. For some women, it may increase the risk of:</p><ul><li>Blood clots</li><li>Heart attack</li><li>Stroke</li><li>Breast cancer</li><li>Gallbladder disease</li></ul><p>The level of risk depends on the type of hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span>, how long it is used, and your medical history and lifestyle.</p><p>You and your provider should talk about the risks and benefits. If you decide to use hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span>, it is usually recommended to use the lowest dose that helps and for the shortest time needed. Ask your provider how often you should follow up. Many recommend checking in every three to six months at first, then once a year after <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> is working well. </p><p>Food and Drug Administration</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/alcoholusedisorderaudtreatment.html">
      <content name="title">Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatment</span></span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Alcohol Abuse <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatment</span></span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Alcoholism <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatment</span></span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is an alcohol use disorder?<p>An alcohol use disorder (AUD) is drinking that causes distress and harm. It is a medical condition in which you:</p><ul><li>Drink alcohol compulsively</li><li>Can't control how much you drink</li><li>Feel anxious, irritable, and/or stressed when you are not drinking</li></ul><p>An AUD can range from mild to severe, depending on the symptoms. Severe AUD is sometimes called alcoholism or alcohol dependence.</p>What are the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> for alcohol use disorder?<p>Most people with an alcohol use disorder can benefit from some form of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>. Medical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> include medicines and behavioral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span>. For many people, using both types gives them the best results. People who are getting <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> for AUD may also find it helpful to go to a support group such as Alcoholics Anonymous (AA). If you have an AUD and a mental illness, it is important to get <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> for both.</p><p>Some people may need intensive <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> for AUD. They may go to a residential <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> center for rehabilitation (rehab). <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatment</span></span></span> there is highly structured. It usually includes several different kinds of behavioral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span>. It may also include medicines for detox (medical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> for alcohol withdrawal) and/or for treating the AUD.</p>Which medicines can <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treat</span></span></span> alcohol use disorder?<p>Three medicines are approved to <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treat</span></span></span> AUD:</p><ul><li>Disulfiram causes unpleasant symptoms such as nausea and skin flushing whenever you drink alcohol. Knowing that drinking will cause these unpleasant effects may help you stay away from alcohol.</li><li>Naltrexone blocks the receptors in your brain that make you feel good when you drink alcohol. It can also reduce your craving for alcohol. This can help you cut back on your drinking.</li><li>Acamprosate helps you avoid alcohol after you have quit drinking. It works on multiple brain systems to reduce your cravings, especially just after you have quit drinking.</li></ul><p>Your health care provider can help you figure out if one of these medicines is right for you. They are not addictive, so you don't have to worry about trading one addiction for another. They are not a cure, but they can help you manage AUD. This is just like taking medicines to manage a chronic disease such as asthma or diabetes.</p>Which behavioral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies can treat</span></span></span> alcohol use disorder?<p>Another name for behavioral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span> for AUD is alcohol counseling. It involves working with a health care professional to identify and help change the behaviors that lead to your heavy drinking.:</p><ul><li>Cognitive-behavioral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> (CBT) helps you identify the feelings and situations that can lead to heavy drinking. It teaches you coping skills, including how to manage stress and how to change the thoughts that cause you to want to drink. You may get CBT one-on-one with a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapist</span></span></span> or in small groups.</li><li>Motivational enhancement <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> helps you build and strengthen the motivation to change your drinking behavior. It includes about four sessions over a short period of time. The <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> starts with identifying the pros and cons of seeking <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>. Then you and your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapist</span></span></span> work on forming a plan for making changes in your drinking. The next sessions focus on building up your confidence and developing the skills you need to be able to stick to the plan.</li><li>Marital and family counseling includes spouses and other family members. It can help to repair and improve your family relationships. Studies show that strong family support through family <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> may help you to stay away from drinking.</li><li>Brief interventions are short, one-on-one or small-group counseling sessions. It includes one to four sessions. The counselor gives you information about your drinking pattern and potential risks. The counselor works with you to set goals and provide ideas that may help you make a change.</li></ul>Is <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> for alcohol use disorder effective?<p>For most people, <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> for an AUD is helpful. But overcoming an alcohol use disorder is an ongoing process, and you may relapse (start drinking again). You should look at relapse as a temporary setback, and keep trying. Many people repeatedly try to cut back or quit drinking, have a setback, then try to quit again. Having a relapse does not mean that you cannot recover. If you do relapse, it is important to return to <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> right away, so you can learn more about your relapse triggers and improve your coping skills. This may help you be more successful the next time.</p><p>NIH: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/canceralternativetherapies.html">
      <content name="title">Cancer Alternative <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Therapies</span></span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Alternative <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Therapy</span></span></span> for Cancer</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are complementary and alternative <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span> for cancer care?<p>You have many choices to make about your cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>. One choice you might consider is using complementary and alternative medicine (CAM). CAM is the term for medical products and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span> that are not part of standard medical care.</p><p>CAM for cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> involves caring for your mind, body, and spirit. Some methods focus on your breathing or body movements to help you relax. Other CAM <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span> may use special foods, supplements, or diets. Examples of CAM <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span> include acupuncture, chiropractic, and herbal medicines.</p><p>CAM claims can sound promising, but often, researchers don't know how safe some are or how well they work. Studies are ongoing to find out the safety and usefulness of many of these methods.</p>How are complementary and alternative <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span> used for cancer care?<p>If you're thinking about using CAM along with your standard care, it's called integrative medicine. Some methods, such as acupuncture, might help with nausea, pain, and other side effects of cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>.</p><p>A few reasons that people with cancer may use CAM include to:</p><ul><li>Help cope with the side effects of cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span></li><li>Ease worries about cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> and related stress</li><li>Feel that they are doing something more to help their care</li></ul><p>CAM <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> don't work for everyone. Some products might interact with your other medicines. Talk to your health care provider about all the different types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> you use. Your provider can help you make sure that everything you're using for your cancer care works well together.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/opioidusedisorderoudtreatment.html">
      <content name="title">Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatment</span></span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Opioid Abuse and Addiction <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatment</span></span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD)</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are opioids?<p>Opioids, sometimes called narcotics, are a type of drug. They include strong prescription pain relievers, such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, fentanyl, and tramadol. The illegal drug heroin is also an opioid.</p><p>A health care provider may give you a prescription opioid to reduce pain after you have had a major injury or surgery. You may get them if you have severe pain from health conditions like cancer. Some health care providers prescribe them for chronic pain.</p><p>Prescription opioids used for pain relief are generally safe when taken for a short time and as prescribed by your provider. However, opioid use disorder (OUD) is still a possible risk.</p>What is opioid use disorder (OUD)?<p>Opioid use disorder (OUD) means that you have a problematic pattern of using opioids. The pattern causes a lot of distress and impairment (meaning that it causes problems in and interferes with your daily life). Instead of OUD, sometimes people use the terms "opioid dependence" and "opioid addiction." Dependence means feeling withdrawal symptoms when not taking the drug. Addiction is a chronic brain disease that causes a person to compulsively seek out drugs, even though they cause harm. </p>What are the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> for opioid use disorder (OUD)?<p><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatments</span></span></span> for OUD include:</p><ul><li>Medicines; this kind of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> is known as medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD)</li><li>Counseling and behavioral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span></li><li>Residential and hospital-based <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span></li></ul>Which medicines <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treat</span></span></span> opioid opioid use disorder (OUD)?<p>The medicines used in MOUD are methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone:</p><ul><li><p>Methadone, buprenorphine, and lofexidine, which can decrease withdrawal symptoms and cravings. They work by acting on one or another of the targets in the brain that opioids act on. But these medicines are different because they do not make you feel high. Some people worry that if they take methadone or buprenorphine, it means that they are substituting one addiction for another. But it is not; these medicines are a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>. They restore balance to the parts of the brain affected by addiction. This allows your brain to heal while you work toward recovery.</p><p>You may safely take these medicines for months, years, or even a lifetime. If you want to stop taking them, do not do it on your own. You should contact your provider first, and together you can work out a plan for stopping.</p></li><li><p>Naltrexone works differently than methadone and buprenorphine. It does not help you with withdrawal symptoms or cravings. Instead, it takes away the high that you would normally get when you take opioids. Because of this, you would take naltrexone to prevent a relapse, not to try to get off opioids. You have to be off opioids for at least 7-10 days before you can take naltrexone. Otherwise you could have bad withdrawal symptoms.</p></li><li><p>A combination drug that includes buprenorphine and naloxone. Naloxone is a drug to <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treat</span></span></span> an opioid overdose. If you take it along with buprenorphine, you will be less likely to misuse the buprenorphine.</p></li></ul>How does counseling help <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treat</span></span></span> opioid use disorder (OUD)?<p>Counseling for OUD can help you:</p><ul><li>Change your attitudes and behaviors related to drug use</li><li>Build healthy life skills</li><li>Stick with other forms of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>, such as medicines</li></ul><p>There are different types of counseling for OUD, including:</p><ul><li>Individual counseling, which may include setting goals, talking about setbacks, and celebrating progress. You may also talk about legal concerns and family problems. Counseling often includes specific behavioral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span>, such as</li><ul><li>Cognitive-behavioral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> (CBT), which helps you recognize and stop negative patterns of thinking and behavior. It teaches you coping skills, including how to manage stress and change the thoughts that cause you to want to misuse opioids.</li><li>Motivational enhancement <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span>, which helps you build up motivation to stick with your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> plan.</li><li>Contingency management, which focuses on giving you incentives for positive behaviors such as staying off the opioids.</li></ul><li>Group counseling, which can help you feel that you are not alone with your issues. You get a chance to hear about the difficulties and successes of others who have the same challenges. This can help you learn new strategies for dealing with the situations you may come across.</li><li>Family counseling, which includes partners or spouses and other family members who are close to you. It can help to repair and improve your family relationships.</li></ul><p>Counselors can also refer you to other resources that you might need, such as:</p><ul><li>Peer support groups, including 12-step programs like Narcotics Anonymous</li><li>Spiritual and faith-based groups</li><li>HIV testing and hepatitis screening</li><li>Case or care management</li><li>Employment or educational supports</li><li>Organizations that help you find housing or transportation</li></ul>What are residential and hospital-based <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> for opioid use disorder (OUD)?<p>Residential programs combine housing and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> services. You are living with your peers, and you can support each other to stay in recovery. Inpatient hospital-based programs combine health care and OUD <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> services for people with medical problems. Hospitals may also offer intensive outpatient <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>. All these types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> are very structured, and usually include several different kinds of counseling and behavioral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapies</span></span></span>. They usually also include MOUD.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/rehabilitation.html">
      <content name="title">Rehabilitation</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Occupational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Therapy</span></span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Physical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Therapy</span></span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Rehab</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is rehabilitation?<p>Rehabilitation is care that can help you get back, keep, or improve abilities that you need for daily life. These abilities may be physical, mental, and/or cognitive (thinking and learning). You may have lost them because of a disease or injury, or as a side effect from a medical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>. Rehabilitation can improve your daily life and functioning.</p>Who needs rehabilitation?<p>Rehabilitation is for people who have lost abilities that they need for daily life. Some of the most common causes include:</p><ul><li>Injuries and trauma, including burns, fractures (broken bones), traumatic brain injury, and spinal cord injuries</li><li>Stroke</li><li>Severe infections</li><li>Major surgery</li><li>Side effects from medical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span>, such as from cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span></li><li>Certain birth defects and genetic disorders</li><li>Developmental disabilities</li><li>Chronic pain, including back and neck pain</li></ul>What are the goals of rehabilitation?<p>The overall goal of rehabilitation is to help you get your abilities back and regain independence. But the specific goals are different for each person. They depend on what caused the problem, whether the cause is ongoing or temporary, which abilities you lost, and how severe the problem is. For example,:</p><ul><li>A person who has had a stroke may need rehabilitation to be able to dress or bathe without help</li><li>An active person who has had a heart attack may go through cardiac rehabilitation to try to return to exercising</li><li>Someone with a lung disease may get pulmonary rehabilitation to be able to breathe better and improve their quality of life</li></ul>What happens in a rehabilitation program?<p>When you get rehabilitation, you often have a team of different health care providers helping you. They will work with you to figure out your needs, goals, and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> plan. The types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments that may be in a treatment</span></span></span> plan include:</p><ul><li>Assistive devices, which are tools, equipment, and products that help people with disabilities move and function</li><li>Cognitive rehabilitation <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> to help you relearn or improve skills such as thinking, learning, memory, planning, and decision making</li><li>Mental health counseling</li><li>Music or art <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> to help you express your feelings, improve your thinking, and develop social connections</li><li>Nutritional counseling</li><li>Occupational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> to help you with your daily activities</li><li>Physical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> to help your strength, mobility, and fitness</li><li>Recreational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> to improve your emotional well-being through arts and crafts, games, relaxation training, and animal-assisted <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span></li><li>Speech-language <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span> to help with speaking, understanding, reading, writing and swallowing</li><li><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatment</span></span></span> for pain</li><li>Vocational rehabilitation to help you build skills for going to school or working at a job</li></ul><p>Depending on your needs, you may have rehabilitation in the providers' offices, a hospital, or an inpatient rehabilitation center. In some cases, a provider may come to your home. If you get care in your home, you will need to have family members or friends who can come and help with your rehabilitation.</p></content>
